content: Meningococcal disease is an illness caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis. This bacterium is transmitted from person to person through close personal contact, such as living in the same household or kissing. Individuals who develop meningococcal disease require immediate medical intervention, as the condition can progress rapidly and become life-threatening. The symptoms of meningococcal disease depend on the specific type of illness. When the bacteria infect the meninges (the protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord), the condition is referred to as meningococcal meningitis. Common symptoms of meningococcal meningitis include the sudden onset of fever, severe headache, and a stiff neck. Additional symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, heightened sensitivity to light (photophobia), and confusion. In infants and young children, the signs may differ and include lethargy, irritability, vomiting, or poor reflexes. In some cases, the bacteria can enter the bloodstream, leading to a condition known as meningococcal septicemia. Symptoms of septicemia include extreme fatigue, vomiting, chills, severe muscle or joint pain, rapid breathing, diarrhea, and the appearance of a dark-colored rash. Meningococcal disease can result in death within a matter of hours if not treated promptly. Certain populations are at higher risk of contracting meningococcal disease. While anyone can be affected, individuals living in or traveling to specific regions are more susceptible. The meningitis belt in sub-Saharan Africa has the highest incidence of meningococcal disease globally, particularly during the dry season from December to June. Travelers who spend extended periods with local populations in this region, especially during outbreaks, are at increased risk. Additionally, participants in the Hajj or Umrah pilgrimages in Saudi Arabia are at heightened risk of contracting the disease. Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing meningococcal disease. In the United States, two types of meningococcal vaccines are available: the MenACWY vaccine, which protects against serogroups A, C, W, and Y, and the MenB vaccine, which targets serogroup B. The MenACWY vaccine is routinely administered to pre-teens and teenagers. It is recommended that all children aged 11 to 12 years receive a dose of the MenACWY vaccine, followed by a booster shot at age 16. Adolescents and young adults aged 16 to 18 may also receive the MenB vaccine. Younger children and adults may require the MenACWY vaccine depending on their travel plans or specific risk factors. Some individuals who have previously been vaccinated may need a booster dose to maintain protection. It is important to note that it takes approximately 7 to 10 days after vaccination for the body to develop maximum immunity against the disease. For those traveling to Saudi Arabia for the Hajj or Umrah pilgrimages, proof of MenACWY vaccination is mandatory. This vaccine may also be referred to as the tetravalent or quadrivalent meningococcal vaccine. Currently, there are no specific recommendations for receiving the MenB vaccine before travel.
